items.title: Buckle Up: The Final 3 Weeks of the Campaign Are Gonna Be Some Kind of UGLY
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
We’ve endured some very dark days in Trump II, but yesterday was particularly grim — and a possible taste of what’s to come between now and Election Day.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth exuberantly announced that the holiday season execution by firing squad of former Army Major Nidal Malik Hasan for the Ft. Hood shooting will be live-streamed.

In New York City, an ICE agent shot and wounded a Dominican national who was in his car with his 5-year-old child in the backseat.

In a televised debate in the Michigan Senate race, GOP nominee Mike Rogers used Islamophobic smears to baselessly associate Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with terrorism — after which President Trump called El-Sayed a “Terrorist Sympathizer” in a social media post.

Somehow, the Michigan Senate debate was worse than the Georgia Senate debate, where GOP nominee Rep. Mike Collins has so many ties to neo-Nazis that it’s hard to keep count, prompting Sen. Jon Ossoff to scoff that Collins had “hired half the Third Reich” in his congressional office.

Against that backdrop, the Trump DOJ is actively seeking to vindictively prosecute former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson for allegedly lying to Congress as the star witness in the Jan. 6 committee hearings.

While the chaos of Trump II is often erratic and unpredictable, yesterday’s events are all tied to the upcoming election one way or the other. Even the ICE shooting came only two days after ICE increased its daily quota back to 3,000 arrests a day ahead of the midterms. The collective desperation of Trump and the GOP to avert a disastrous electoral defeat is likely to produce some even darker days over the next three and half weeks.

The Persecution of Cassidy Hutchinson

The vindictive prosecution of Cassidy Hutchinson is being improbably spearheaded by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. It would normally have absolutely no role in pursuing this kind of case, but the division is led by the ambitious Harmeet Dhillon, who is eager to audition for a promotion.

Dhillon’s team began presenting purported evidence against Hutchinson to a D.C. federal grand jury this week. While most of the reports cast it as investigation into whether Hutchison lied to Congress, the Washington Post, citing an unnamed source, suggests there maybe a twist: “[P]rosecutors have been exploring charging Hutchinson with a civil rights violation, potentially bringing a more unusual case than a simple charge of lying to Congress, one of the people familiar said.”

In Other Vindictive Prosecution News …

A federal judge has cleared the way for Kseniia Petrova to conduct discovery into whether she was the victim of vindictive prosecution by the Trump administration. Petrova is the Harvard researcher who was detained at Boston’s Logan International Airport in February 2025 and later charged with smuggling for bringing frog embryo samples into the country for her research.

New Info on Kurt Olsen’s Failed Polygraph

The exact circumstances of the failed polygraph of Trump DOJ official Kurt Olsen keep dribbling out. The latest, from the New York Times (emphasis mine):

It turned out he had failed a polygraph test about his contacts with foreigners, which imperiled his security clearance, according to two people familiar with the matter. Mr. Olsen said he complied with all requirements regarding foreign contacts and had not resigned over his clearance, but declined to say more.

With everything else going on, the Kimberly Guilfoyle scandal is almost a welcome relief — a Molière comedy of the Trump era.

The official responses to the Wall Street Journal blockbuster were quite unimpressive.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio spewed a lot of bluster in refusing to answer any questions about his ambassador to Greece — but he also offered no defense of Kimberly Guilfoyle:

Vice President JD Vance was similarly unenthusiastic about rushing to Guilfoyle’s defense:

Bad News for Kim: Loose Cannon Is Talking

If there’s one thing to know about the latest Guilfoyle scandal, it’s that her accuser doesn’t exactly fit the profile of the most reliable narrator. So the WSJ really had to bring the receipts, as it describes here.

Making matters worse for her is that her accuser seems to love the spotlight and spent the day talking to damn near any TV news outlet that would listen.

With so few Trump scandals truly breaking through into the broader cultural zeitgeist, Guilfoyle’s brazenness, shamelessness, and sloppiness have combined to potentially make her the rare exception.

Have a Good Holiday Weekend

See you back here Tuesday.

items.title: New Details Emerge on Stephen Miller's Meddling at the Trump DOJ
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
The Tip of the Politicization Spear

Since the dawn of Trump II, Stephen Miller has been the barely hidden hand running the Justice Department from the White House. Now a new report from CBS News adds quite a bit more detail to the level of influence and control that Miller exerts over the Trump DOJ.

The story is framed around an apparent conflict of interest. Miller attended an counterterrorism training session at FBI headquarters on Sept. 29 that was focused on President Trump’s notorious NSPM-7 on domestic terrorism and political violence. Miller urged the federal agents in attendance to be more aggressive in pursuing threats against government officials and their families — at the same time he was an alleged victim and potential witness in a case of alleged threats to his wife, Katie. Miller was reportedly frustrated by the pace of the criminal investigation into the allegedly threatening communications.

“In his comments, Miller spoke about the need for federal law enforcement agents to be more proactive in investigating threat cases and told them that no case is too small, whether the threats are directed toward a congressman, a spouse, friends, loved ones or a speaker at a college campus, the senior FBI official said,” according to CBS News.

The top two FBI agents in the counterterrorism division of the FBI Washington Field Office were demoted last month over “frustration shared by the Miller family” that the Katie Miller case was moving too slowly. Their demotions reportedly factored into the resignation of FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey, although the FBI publicly dimissed that reporting as “fake news.”

Two days after Miller spoke to federal agents at the training session, a Massachusetts man was indicted for cyberstalking on Oct. 1 — despite reported concerns from career prosecutors in Boston that his communications to Katie Miller didn’t amount to a federal crime. He was charged with using interstate communications with the intent to harass and intimidate by sending her at least 40 calls, voicemails, and text messages in August and September, some of them crude and profane.

But a glaring conflict of interest is just one element of this story, and probably not the most important one.

Notably, this episode appears to be a subset of the Trump administration’s broader push to lump all threats together with legitimate political opposition and brand them as domestic terrorism. The criminalization of political opposition to Trump is one of the darkest through-lines of his second term.

In this episode, two things jump out: (i) Miller picked a counterterrorism training session to urge more aggressive action in cases involving threats and harassment, citing the assassination of Charlie Kirk; and (ii) Katie Miller’s alleged cyberstalker was “arrested by members of the F.B.I.’s joint terrorism task force, an unusual show of force for a cyberstalking case,” the NYT noted last week.

In other words, what might have normally been a local law enforcement matter is now federalized and turned into a counterterrorism investigation. The Trump White House went so far as to defend Miller’s presence at the training session on domestic terrorism grounds, telling CBS News that Miller is tasked with carrying out the NSPM-7 mandate to “investigate, disrupt, and dismantle all stages of organized political violence and domestic terrorism.”

The other big picture issue is the one Morning Memo keeps coming back to: the mind-blowing fact of an unabashedly political White House aide addressing federal agents at FBI headquarters. The DOJ, including the FBI, being run out of the White House remains the defining corrupt act of the Trump II presidency.

The CBS News story — co-bylined by Sarah N. Lynch, a superb reporter on the DOJ beat — goes quite a bit further in revealing how involved Miller is in the running of the Justice Department:

  • In an earlier episode, Miller pressured the DOJ to take action against a Virginia political activist who protested outside of the Millers’ Arlington home and distributed their address on flyers. A federal magistrate judge twice rejected search warrant applications in the case, CBS News previously reported.

  • In the Virginia case, Miller asked FBI counterterrorism agents in his neighborhood’s political activist group and regularly called the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the the Eastern District of Virginia for updates.

  • Miller has been holding monthly meetings with the heads of federal law enforcement agencies about the deployments of the National Guard and federal agents to D.C. and Memphis in Trump’s “violent crime crackdown.”

  • “Miller is also in touch multiple times a week with the Deputy Attorney General’s office to discuss fraud and immigration cases, according to sources with direct knowledge of the matter,” according to CBS News. The DAG is essentially the chief operations officer at DOJ and runs the department day to day.

Miller’s meddling (which may be too weak of word) at DOJ is truly unprecedented. He is the tip of Trump’s spear aimed at politicizing the Justice Department.

Kurt Olsen Reportedly Failed a Polygraph

Kurt Olsen — the Big Lie proponent who stepped down as the lead prosecutor in the bogus investigation into a “grand conspiracy” by the Deep State to deprive Donald Trump of his civil rights — had his DOJ security clearance terminated last month after failing a polygraph test, Reuters reports.

‘I Can Do Whatever I Want, If I Want’

  • The American Prospect: In an important development, U.S. District Judge John C. Hinderaker, a Trump appointee in Arizona, has ordered DHS to “facilitate” the return to the United States of an Egyptian man that it deported to Equatorial Guinea, a country where he has no ties. As reporter Gillian Brockell notes, the ruling “could have far-reaching implications for thousands of others subjected to the Trump administration’s third-country removal scheme.”

  • Washington Sun: In a ruling this week, U.S. District Judge Gary R. Brown, a Trump appointee in Brooklyn, condemned ICE agents for falsifying records to cover up a pair of bad arrests. “The evidence suggests that ICE attempted to support their unsupported misidentification argument through false or misleading documentation and testimony,” Brown concluded.

  • CNN: ICE told agents nationwide on Tuesday to increase immigration arrests by 1,000 people per day, returning to a previous goal of 3,000 daily arrests.

“On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day. But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking.”—Randy Spivey, a lawyer for Christa Pike, on her recovery from Tennessee’s attempted execution

The Corruption: Kimberly Guilfoyle Edition

The WSJ manages to outdo its remarkable story last month on Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and former fiancée of Don Jr., with a follow-up bombshell.

I started to summarize the highlights, but I really can’t do it justice. Just go read it.

items.title: Desperate GOP Scrambles to Defend Once-Solid Red Seats
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Republican political consultants are practically falling over each other to make the most dire pronouncements about the GOP’s fate in the midterms.

“If the bottom continues falling out like it has been, this will be worse than 2006,” one national Republican strategist tells Politico. Democrats picked up 31 seats that year and ended 12 years of GOP control of the House.

I’m deeply skeptical of poll-driven narratives in election coverage — which the past few cycles have only reinforced — but there’s quite a bit more to go on than just public opinion surveys in assessing the state of the midterms. Between now and Election Day, I’ll be frequently including in Morning Memo a sampling of those additional data points: which races are being newly contested and which aren’t, where the spending is going and where it’s not, and other markers on the state of the race — including President Trump’s unscripted intemperate outbursts.

The Cook Political Report on Tuesday moved three Senate races in Democrats’ favor:

  • Kansas from Lean Republican to Toss Up

  • North Carolina from Lean Democrat to Likely Democrat

  • New Hampshire from Toss Up to Lean Democrat

In deep-red South Carolina, appointed Sen. Darline Graham (R) is struggling to hold on to her late brother’s seat, forcing the Senate Leadership Fund to dump $5 million into her race against Dr. Annie Andrews. In a sign of the brewing trouble for the GOP, Trump went on a “crazed, manic tirade” this week against Andrews, using an anti-trans slur among other attacks.

On the House side, in a sign of increasing desperation, Republicans have quietly resumed backing Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) despite earlier calls from within the party for him to drop out of the race amidst allegations against him of domestic abuse.

Election Ratfuckery Alert

The Trump administration continues to pull levers and push buttons to try to abuse the power of the federal government to swing the election its way:

  • The Department of Homeland Security has investigated more than 150 voter registration groups in search of evidence that they’re helping noncitizens illegally register to vote, according to internal documents obtained via FOIA and provided to the New York Times. The DHS effort has been most heavily focused on groups in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. DHS has considered using undercover agents in its investigations, the documents reveal. Also of note:

The documents also reveal that Heather Honey, a prominent 2020 election denier who now serves as the department’s point person on “election integrity,” provided 48.4 million records of unknown provenance to federal investigators who are trying to find noncitizens on the voter rolls.

  • The Trump DOJ dispatched federal prosecutors and an FBI agent to monitor polls in Maricopa and Pima counties in Arizona during its July primary election — a dramatic departure from past DOJ practice of using Civil Rights Division personnel as poll monitors to avoid intimidating voters and local election officials, Democracy Docket reports. The Trump DOJ is apparently planning to continue using prosecutors as poll monitors in the general election, telling Democracy Docket that “department attorneys, including prosecutors, will serve as election monitors.”

  • In the run-up to election, ICE has begun asking detainees if they have ever voted illegally and, if so, whether in person or by mail, the WaPo reports. “ICE reviews credible allegations of potential criminal activity within its jurisdiction, including allegations related to election integrity,” an ICE spokesperson told the newspaper.

The Big Lie Crazies Still Big Lie-ing

Big Lie purveyor Tina Peters met with President Trump in the Oval Office this week to discuss “election integrity.” Meanwhile, election denier Cleta Mitchell is “pushing a scheme to have Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick seize voting machines,” Democracy Docket reports. Former Trump DOJ official Ed Martin helpfully ties all of this together:

: All of this comes as the Trump DOJ continues to fight to enforce a grand jury subpoena of Fulton County, Georgia, for the names and personal information of the hundreds of staffers, contractors, and volunteers who worked on the 2020 election. Jan. 6 never ends.

How Trump Can Still Subvert the Election

Election law expert Rick Hasen gives a fairly glowing assessment of how well the guardrails have held so far against Trump’s assault on free and fair midterm elections — and assesses where the greatest risks remain.

Another Classic Trump Con

Trump’s claim that he and his super PAC will start paying for the pro-Trump TV ads that the taxpayer funds have been used to air during the stretch run of the midterms that he will reimburse the government for the expenses it already incurred.

“White House officials clarified on Tuesday to Politico that the president’s post did not mean the PAC would pay for the spots that had already aired,” Politico reports.

More than $10 million of a $20 million DHS contract has already been spent on the ads, the NYT calculates.

  • : Last year, when he was acting deputy attorney general, Emil Bove pressed the FBI to illegally investigate ICE protesters in Los Angeles in violation of their constitutional rights and bureau policy, an FBI whistleblower alleges. The allegations emerged in a whistleblower complaint to leaders of the Senate Judiciary Committee by Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s LA field office. Fields also claims that FBI Director Kash Patel succumbed to pressure from the White House to investigate another group of ICE protesters after President Trump saw them in TikTok post.

  • : After purging career lawyers, the Trump DOJ’s once-prestigous Civil Rights Division — led by Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon — is turning to partisans and conspiracists to fill its depleted ranks, the NYT reports.

  • : Lawyers for David Hearn, the man wrongly accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool, sent a letter to the inspectors general of DOJ and DOI asking for an investigation of the circumstances of his arrest and subsequently dismissed prosecution. Among his lawyers is Michael R. Bromwich, a former DOJ IG.

EU Preps for Mass Casualty Russian Attack

In a restricted, closed-door meeting last Wednesday, EU ambassadors discussed how to respond collectively to a hybrid Russian attack that results in mass casualties, a risk they fear looks increasingly likely, Politico reports.

“[W]hen a majority of the justices on our highest court show themselves to be consistently indifferent to the growing chasm between law and justice, it is not ‘public rhetoric’ that causes Americans to distrust the Court. It is the Court that surrenders its own legitimacy in the eyes of the public.”—

items.title: Court Ruling Hobbles Trump DOJ’s Jihad Against Elusive Threat of Noncitizen Voting
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Judge Strikes Down Federal Ban on Noncitizen Voting

In a potentially very important ruling last week, a federal judge in south Florida concluded that the Trump administration’s effort to prosecute noncitizen voting relies on a 40-year-old federal statute that is unconstitutional.

In dismissing the prosecution of a Jamaican national for illegally voting in the 2020 election, U.S. District Judge David Leibowitz (a Biden appointee) found 18 U.S.C. § 611, which outlaws voting by noncitizens in federal elections, to be a “voter qualification statute.” As such, Congress intruded on the power of the states to determine voter qualifications by passing the law outlawing noncitizen voting.

“[T]he Constitution does not authorize Congress to legislate voter qualifications for federal elections,” Leibowitz ruled. “Congress has no power to say vote or vote in federal elections—that foundational power is reserved for the States, and limits Congress.”

As Politico’s Kyle Cheney notes, the statute that Judge Leibowitz invalidated underpins several Trump administration noncitizen-voting prosecutions that it ramped up ahead of the midterm elections:

Yet in dozens of other recent cases, announced with great fanfare by the Justice Department — often accompanied by photographs of people being arrested by Homeland Security agents — the administration is hanging its illegal voting crackdown on this very statute. Many are slated for trial in December and January.

Judge Leibowitz was the first judge to ever rule on the constitutionality of the statute. To help reach his decision, Judge Leibowitz had appointed Supreme Court litigator Paul Clement as a friend of the court to advise him on the constitutionality of Congress enacting the 18 U.S.C. § 61.

Given the paucity of noncitizen voting, the broader import of Judge Leibowitz’s ruling is that it undermines the Trump propaganda machine’s focus on noncitizen voting as a catch-all Big Lie that seeks to justify the federal takeover of elections, the imposition of new restrictions on voting, especially mail-in voting, and the delegitimization of elections generally.

  • ProPublica: More than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in the Trump administration’s mass deportation dragnet.

  • TPM’s Hunter Walker: An ICE challenge coin for sale on eBay is emblazoned with the slogan: “There is no hunting like the hunting of man.” It’s not clear whether the coin was officially issued by ICE.

“… if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere. Anywhere.”—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), in a closed-door fundraiser, on the progressive movement’s “generational” chance to “break the map” of American politics

Will Dems Pull a McConnell on SCOTUS?

Some Senate Democrats are threatening not to confirm any Trump nominees to the Supreme Court for the rest of his term — if they win the Senate majority next month.

Jay Willis: The Conservative Takeover of SCOTUSblog Is Just What the Supreme Court Needed

  • : The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals quickly scheduled oral arguments for Oct. 23 on whether the president can fire court-appointed U.S. attorneys — a part of his scheme to install loyalists as the top federal prosecutors in blue states. The appeal by the Trump administration comes in the case of Roger Rogoff, the court-appointed U.S. attorney in Seattle, whose firing was ruled unlawful by a federal judge from outside the district. In related news, Rogoff has agreed to staying the lower court order and to not taking office while the appeal is pending.

  • : President Trump and his former co-defendants in the Mar-a-Lago documents case are asking the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals to delay oral arguments on whether Judge Aileen Cannon’s order permanently sealing Volume II of Special Counsel Jack Smith’s report should be overturned. In the new filing, attorneys say they need the delay because of scheduling conflicts and because they need time to confer with President Trump. The oral arguments had been rescheduled multiple times over the past several months, most recently for January, but then last week was abruptly moved up to Nov. 2, the day before the midterm elections.

Trump Nixes Politico From Press Pool

The Trump White House barred Politico from boarding Air Force One for a Monday trip to Nebraska, which prevented it from serving in the presidential press pool. The White House similarly retaliated against CNN over the weekend. Along with MS Now, Politico and CNN previously went to court to overturn a Trump ban on the three outlets from accessing the White House.

Trump Claims He’ll Pay for Pro-Trump Ads

In an apparent reversal, President Trump posted on social media that he and his PAC will pay for the series of four pro-Trump TV ads being aired during the stretch run of midterm election and originally paid for by the federal government.

More than $10 million in taxpayer-funded ads have run since September under a $20 million DHS contract, according to the NYT.

“It was unclear if the PAC would repay the U.S. government for the money already spent or just pay for ads going forward,” the WSJ reported.

US Feared Drone Attack On Bombers in UK

The abrupt retreat of a dozen B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford to their home base in the U.S. came in response to intel that Iran was planning a sophisticated drone attack on the planes and their crews.

On Guard On NATO’s Eastern Flank

Politico: Lithuanian PM calls for NATO plan to counter Russia’s hybrid attacks

The Global March of the Far Right

  • : In once again elevating the Bolsonaro clan in Sunday’s election, Brazil gave the far right its most decisive victory since the country’s military dictatorship ended in 1985, Harvard’s Elizabeth McKenna writes.

  • : Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany party was elected as president of the parliament in Saxony-Anhalt, the first time since the Nazi era that a far-right politician was elected to lead a state legislature.

The Televangelist Origins of Donald Trump

The death of disgraced (is there any other kind?) televangelist Jim Bakker at age 86 lets us dip back in for a moment to the gaudy nouveau riche aesthetics of the mid-1980s out of which came endless TV preacher scandals and ultimately the public persona of Donald Trump.

I used to think that the Trump aesthetic mirrored the Jim Bakkers and the Jimmy Swaggarts because they all peaked in the 1980s, which happened to coincide with the glory days of high-glam primetime soaps, which set an unfortunate standard for opulence. But I’ve come to see Trump as a secular televangelist preaching his own version of the prosperity gospel to the same marks susceptible to the same grift that powered the fleeting televangelical fortunes.

Trump’s grift has been bigger and bolder, managing somehow not to have his own soul saved and or to heed a call to follow Jesus, yet being fully embraced by evangelical ministers, often literally in performative Oval Office prayer sessions. Grift knows grift.

items.title: With Four Weeks to Go, Dems Are in the Driver’s Seat
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
With voting coming to a close four weeks from tomorrow, Morning Memo will be shifting its focus to the midterms, with dual track coverage of the horse race and the outsized expectations for Democrats as an opposition party, if they win.

Usually at this point in the election cycle, expectations management is focused on not being so confident that it dampens your voters’ sense of urgency to get to the polls, mutes the post-election news coverage of your victory, and takes the edge off the mandate you win.

But this cycle Democrats are saddled with enormously unrealistic expectations about what they can and should do the election. Even if they win both chambers of Congress, Democrats even in normal times would face structural, institutional, and political limitations that are very real and will make achieving quick, tangible, meaningful reform virtually impossible.

But these are not normal times.

President Trump has done astonishing damage across all of civic life, in the public and private sectors. He will continue to enjoy the strategic and tactical advantage that comes when you don’t care about collateral damage and when wanton destruction is easier than building enduring institutions.

In addition, many of the ingredients that gave rise to the Trump era remain: a degraded information ecosystem, a fierce right-wing propaganda machine, a nihilistic Republican Party not committed to democracy or to a robust civic life, among many others.

That doesn’t mean the election is not important or that an opposition party can serve no function — but it’s obvious that Democrats will come in shouldering the weight of pressure to move fast and decisively in a system that favors neither. The opposition will also face the unhelpful dichotomy that while the American political system has slid over the edge toward neo-fascism, most of the political press still covers campaigns and elections with the same dated tropes and stale constructs — as if things haven’t fundamentally changed.

It can’t be the case that whether we get democracy or fascism, the rule of law or authoritarianism, reform or systemic corruption rides on the result of each election. Yet, here we are.

Midterm Elections Watch: Senate Edition

  • : The Senate Leadership Fund — the super PAC aligned with the Senate GOP — has paused funding in the North Carolina Senate race and plans to invest $14 million to save Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in Kansas.

  • : Ken Paxton’s estranged wife can’t bring herself to say his name, but in a new ad urges Republicans to vote for the GOP ticket: “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room. In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team. It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line.”

Midterm Elections Watch: House Edition

  • Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee political director Brooke Butler predicts Democrats will carry the House with as many as 240 seats. Democrats have held a House majority that large only once in the last three decades: the high-water mark of 257 seats after the 2008 election.

  • If Republicans lose the House, Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) is likely to run for House minority leader, Punchbowl reports: “Jordan won’t admit it publicly, but his inner circle of aides, advisers and friends is plotting for a leadership election, and he’s discussed it with people close to him.”

Midterm Election Shenanigans Watch

  • The George Election Board’s request for the Trump DOJ to intervene in the state’s voting systems was a rogue act by the board’s executive director, the board chair told Votebeat. More here.

  • Reuters: How Trump’s obsession with ‘rigged’ voting machines spread across US government

  • Contrary to earlier reports, election denier Kurt Olsen is still employed at the Justice Department, according to the Washington Post. The newspaper had previously reported that Olsen resigned not just as head of the “grand conspiracy” investigation in south Florida, but from DOJ entirely:

A message Olsen sent Monday announcing his departure was originally misinterpreted by officials in Washington and Miami as a full resignation from the Justice Department, but Olsen later clarified to his bosses that he still intended to remain a department employee, even though he is no longer attached to the case, one of those people said Wednesday. His current assignment remains unclear.

Shock! Trump Behind Pro-Trump Govt Ads

President Trump was directly involved in ordering the use of $20 million in DHS funds to air TV ads in the stretch run of the midterm elections extolling his presidency, the NYT reports:

Mr. Trump was eager to see the laudatory ads on the air and told Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to come up with the money from within the government, the people said. Mark Paoletta, the budget office’s counsel, and Will Scharf, the White House counsel, both said it would be legal to use D.H.S. funds. The president and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, both spoke with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, about the ads.

“My party is being infiltrated by people like Bo French. Nick Fuentes goes to Dallas and meets with a bunch of Republican leaders. This guy is a Nazi. We’ve got all these people getting on their little podcasts and so forth, saying: ‘We’re just asking questions about the Jews.’”—

TPM’s Christopher Mathias: Chris Rufo — Known For ‘DEI’ and ‘CRT’ Panics — Tries to Make ‘the Indian Question’ a Thing

Judge Blocks Border Wall In Big Bend

A federal judge in El Paso on Friday temporarily blocked construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including the eponymous national park.

  • : Marimar Martínez, the woman shot five times by a Border Patrol agent during Operation Midway Blitz, is expected to file a federal lawsuit today “that includes new ballistics analysis and video animation showing the agent was not in harm’s way when he opened fire,” the Chicago Tribune reports.

  • : DHS agents not only tracked and intimidated people observing ICE activity during Operation Catch of the Day, but allegedly stored information about them in a Palantir-built database, according to newly unsealed court filings reviewed by Wired.

  • : A Hasidic Jew who protested against the Israeli flag may now be deported, the New York Times reports.

US Rushes Bombers Home From UK

NYT: “The United States rushed over the weekend to withdraw all 12 B-1 Air Force bombers from an air base in southern England after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation, two U.S. officials said on Sunday.”

Dennis Hastert, 1942-2026

The longest-serving Republican speaker of the House — who turned out to be, in the words of his sentencing judge, a “serial child molester” — died of natural causes at his Illinois home over the weekend at age 84.

Dennis Hastert served in Congress for 20 years, eight of them as speaker. But it wasn’t until 2015, eight years after he left office, that his abuse decades earlier of wrestlers while he was a wrestling coach emerged. Hastert pleaded guilty to illegally structuring payments to one of his victims and served 13 months in prison.

It remains one of the mysteries of American politics that the Denny Hastert saga — a tragic coda to the corruption of the Tom Delay era — never broke through into the wider political consciousness.

items.title: Bill Pulte Guts the IG Office That Investigated Him
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Cuts Would Put IG Office Out of Business

In a move that smacks of retaliation, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte is moving to slash next year’s budget for the agency’s inspector general’s office by more than 60% — after it was involved in an earlier investigation of him.

The surprise draconian cuts to the IG’s office would eviscerate its ability to conduct investigations, IG staff told Congress in a letter this week: “We will be forced to reduce staffing by approximately 70-80% in FY 2027, which will result in the discontinuance of essentially all criminal investigations conducted by our Office of Investigations.”

(Senate Democrats sent a letter to Pulte yesterday demanding that he restore funding for the IG’s office and also demanded his resignation.)

The shock budget cuts are just a continuation of a retaliation campaign by Pulte against internal watchdogs that’s been going on for a year.

Pulte, who also serves as chairman of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, has had an unusually high profile in Trump II for someone in his position, largely because he led the charge to use bogus claims of mortgage fraud to retaliate against Trump foes, like Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) and Fed Gov. Lisa Cook. With ready access to the president and poster boards often in hand, Pulte offered Trump what he already wanted: a tool of retribution.

Pulte’s mortgage fraud jihad resulted in an internal investigation of Pulte himself over whether he improperly obtained mortgage records of high-profile Democrats officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, the Wall Street Journal reported in November:

Fannie’s ethics and investigations group had received internal complaints alleging senior officials had improperly directed staff to access the mortgage documents of James and others, according to the people. The Fannie investigators were probing to find out who had made the orders, whether Pulte had the authority to seek the documents and whether or not they had followed proper procedure, the people said.

That group elevated the probe about the James documents to the more senior Office of Inspector General for the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the agency that oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and that Pulte heads, the people said. The acting inspector general then passed the report to the U.S. attorney’s office in eastern Virginia, some of the people said.

To summarize, Fannie Mae investigators found enough of concern to bring in higher-ups at the FHFA IG’s office, which took them seriously enough to forward the concerns to federal prosecutors pursuing James.

“The FHFA acting inspector general sent the office the report at least in part because it could be considered material information for James’s defense in the case, one of the people said,” according to the WSJ.

You already know what happened next: James was indicted for mortgage fraud last October in the Eastern District of Virginia by then-acting U.S. Attorney Lindsey Halligan. The indictment was ultimately dismissed by a federal judge because Halligan was unlawfully appointed as U.S. attorney. Subsequent efforts by Halligan to indict James were rejected by two different grand juries.

The fallout from that episode was swift and severe.

Joe Allen, the FHFA acting inspector general who sent the internal investigation to prosecutors, was asked to step down, the WSJ reported. Around the same time, the administration fired about a dozen officials within Fannie Mae’s ethics and internal investigations unit.

The pattern of retaliation is clear. But there’s a more recent wrinkle.

Last week, the WSJ — which you can see has been all over the Pulte story for many months — reported that Pulte hadn’t just targeted Democrats’ mortgages. He’d also examined the mortgages of Todd Blanche!

Blanche and Pulte have been nemeses, for reasons that seem pretty obvious even from the outside looking in. Pulte — a nonlawyer — was stoking Trump’s sense of vengeance with spurious promises of prosecutions that Blanche was stuck with having to try to make happen.

As it was described to WSJ: “Some officials believed Pulte had been trying to collect information on Blanche and others to undermine them and pressure them to more quickly pursue the investigations, the people said.” Pulte denies improperly pulling any internal files.

As if that wasn’t enough, DOJ began its own inquiry into whether Pulte and other officials had “inappropriately shared information about the Justice Department’s investigation into Schiff with those who weren’t authorized to be part of it,” the WSJ reported.

I was immediately intrigued by the anonymous sourcing of the WSJ story. Who would have been in a position to learn that Pulte had targeted Blanche? I came up with two likely candidates: the FHFA IG via Fannie Mae’s investigators and DOJ through its own investigation of the leaks against Schiff.

But that doesn’t mean that the FHFA IG dropped the dime on Pulte to the WSJ. Remember: The FHFA IG already gave the results of its Pulte investigation to DOJ a year ago in the James case. So DOJ was in a position to know in either instance.

Either way, it’s quite a coincidence that a week after that revelation Pulte is taking another retaliatory swing at the FHFA IG and basically trying to put it out of business.

Judge Drives a Stake Thru the Heart of Trump’s US Attorney Scheme

In a major decision that thwarts President Trump’s scheme to appoint loyalist federal prosecutors in blue states, a federal judge ruled that the president cannot fire court-appointed U.S. attorneys.

U.S. District Judge Stanley Bastian issued a preliminary injunction restoring the court-appointed Roger Rogoff as U.S. attorney in Seattle. In his order, Bastian concluded:

Allowing the President to fire a court-appointed U.S. Attorney would upend the framework created by the Constitution and the statutory framework, which together balances the President’s right to appoint and the Senate’s right to confirm. Allowing the President to fire a court-appointed U.S. Attorney also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be conferred by the Senate—in other words, bypassing the requirement that the Executive and Legislative branches work together to nominate and confirm the U.S. Attorney.

The Trump DOJ quickly moved to appeal the preliminary injunction order.

Judge Orders Inquiry Into DOJ in Broadview 6 Case

U.S. District Judge April Perry has commenced an inquiry in the conduct of the Trump DOJ in the Broadview 6 case. She named University of Chicago law professor William Baude, a former clerk for Chief Justice John Roberts, as a friend of the court to take an adversarial position to the Justice Department, since the underlying criminal case has been dismissed and the former defendants cannot play that role.

The Florida Senate race is competitive enough for the vice president to be campaigning there in person, and spewing racist and xenophobic garbage against the Democratic nominee:

Trump’s Post-Election Plan for Bombing Iran Leaves GOPers Exposed

President Trump’s stated plan to delay the resumption of large-scale bombing of Iran until after the midterms is a not-very-well-concealed effort to protect Republicans up for reelection from the political consequences of the unpopular war.

The size and scale of the bombing campaign planned for late November has forced the Pentagon to begin taking active measures to deploy sufficient manpower and materiel to the Middle East, the WSJ reports:

  • The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier deployed from San Diego on Sunday and will be the third carrier strike group in the Middle East when it arrives in late November.

  • The USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group also deployed from California this week, with Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, and will be the second such group in the Middle East when it arrives.

Another way of looking at this is that the threat to resume bombing is a negotiation tactic. The newly deployed forces will eventually relieve existing forces, but their arrival in theater means for a time they U.S will have a particularly robust force with which to either carry out renewed bombing or present a credible threat to do so.

Judge Demands OLC Memo on Boat Strikes

In a ruling Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Paul A. Engelmayer of Manhattan ordered the Trump administration to provide him with the Office of Legal Counsel memo that provides the legal justification for the lawless high seas campaign of strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats.

The order comes in a lawsuit brought by legal groups to enforce their FOIA request for the memo, which the administration is fighting against releasing publicly.

Noting the irony of the administration touting the memo to justify its conduct while refusing to release it, Judge Engelmayer wrote: “The agency defendants cannot claim surprise from this consequence of the Executive Branch’s repeated public statements embracing the OLC Memo—and it only—as setting out the legal parameters for the boat strikes.”

items.title: Trump DOJ Doubles Down on Attacking Judges
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Blanche Targets Minnesota Judges

Under the pretext of an ethics complaint against all but one of the active federal judges in Minnesota, Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled yesterday that not only will the Trump administration continue to run roughshod over the judicial branch but that judges had better shut up about it.

The complaint filed by second and third highest ranking DOJ officials with the uber-right-wing 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is ostensibly about an admittedly unusual decision by the federal judges who bore the brunt of Operation Metro Surge to sit for an interview with the New York Times for a story that ran Sept. 17.

In the interview, the judges — including Patrick Schiltz who was the chief judge during the peak of the flood of mass deportation cases swamping the Minnesota federal court — defended the rule of law, provided a civics lesson on the role of the courts, and described the structural and institutional challenges they had faced. They refrained from talking about individual cases, but they did speak in broad terms about the habeas cases in general, Operation Metro Surge and the conduct of the Trump DOJ.

The complaint — signed by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward — accused the judges of pandering to the press and engaging in unethical behavior that “flagrantly violated” the canons of judicial ethics. It specifically called out Judge Schiltz and Judge John R. Tunheim — who were both quoted by name in the NYT article — for what it called “particularly egregious” misconduct.

The Trump DOJ asked the 8th Circuit to appoint a special committee to conduct an investigation of the judges for their allegedly improper behavior and to order Judges Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves from any cases involving DHS.

The Trump DOJ getting on its high horse about legal ethics is a lot to take on its own. But it’s also striking that the complaint leans into what DOJ officials see as a friendly audience on the 8th Circuit. It emphasizes, for instance, the appeals court’s own decision upholding the Trump administration’s mass detention policy without bond — one of only two appeals courts to do so — in which it overruled the Minnesota judges.

Traditionally, Article III judges have been free to speak publicly on matters of judicial administration, the Constitution, democracy — civics, if you will. They have been free to lobby for more funding, better security protection, restructuring of the judiciary, and reform measures without running afoul of ethics requirements.

But the Trump DOJ — which has defied orders left and right, hidden its worst conduct behind unprepared junior lawyers, botched cases, fired huge numbers of experienced attorneys, and made a hash of the distinguished department — now wants to clamp down on the ability of judges to stand up against what may be the most sustained assault on the judiciary in the nation’s history.

SCOTUS Takes Up Mass Detentions

As expected, the Supreme Court will take up the Trump administration’s policy of mass detention without bond that the circuit courts have split on, but which dozens of judges in thousands of cases have found to be unlawful.

The family of Renee Good who was shot and killed by ICE in January during Operation Metro Surge has filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration arising from her death.

Broadview Six Hearing This Afternoon

A federal judge in Chicago this afternoon will hear arguments over whether to conduct a further inqury into alleged misconduct into Trump’s DOJ’s handling of the grand jury in the Broadview Six case and the aftermath of that now-abandoned prosecution of ICE protesters.

The Supreme Court’s prior handling of the third-country removal case was already the most troublesome emergency docket case, Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck argues, then came this week’s unexplained decision in the case:

“There have certainly been rulings on the emergency docket that I believe to be more clearly and obviously wrong on the merits. And there have been rulings on the emergency docket that have produced even more harmful effects domestically and/or to the separation of powers. But there’s something profoundly ugly about the D.V.D. case that, unfortunately, was on display again on Tuesday.”

Cannon Wiggles Out of Bind

Give her credit: Judge Aileen Cannon has gotten out of the pickle she was in on Volume II of former Special Counsel Jack Smith’s report. She struck a motion from FBI agents who investigated the Mar-a-Lago documents case and are now being targeted by the Trump DOJ seeking clarification on her order sealing Volume II. Her reason: The lawyers had failed to confer with the co-defendants in the underlying criminal case about their motion before filing it.

11th Circuit Stirs to Action

In the Volume II case which is on appeal, the 11th Circuit the appeals court rescheduled oral arguments yet again but moved them earlier for the first time after months of kicking the can down the road. Instead of January of next year they’re now scheduled for the first week of November. Nothing much going on that week.

Reflecting Pool Case Dismissed With Prejudice

Ruling that “no crime occurred,” a DC judge has ruled that the already-dismissed Reflecting Pool case against David Hearn should be dismissed with prejudice, meaning the Trump DOJ can’t bring the case against him again in the future.

“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era. There is no precedent.”—Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, on last night’s horrific attempted execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee.

Pike remains hospitalized this morning. Gov. Bill Lee (R) has halted executions through the end of the year.

items.title: Appeals Courts Slowly Awaken to Trump II Threat
items.author: David Kurtz
items.content:
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back

In the defining legal struggle of our time — whether the federal judiciary will sustain the rule of law long enough to preserve the essential core of a democracy for us to repair, rebuild, and re-enlarge after Trump II — the jury is still out.

Important developments in three different cases yesterday — the Alien Enemies Act, third-country deportations, and Trump’s collusive settlement with the IRS — point in very different directions.

On the face of it, not much unites the cases or offers a common theme or collective takeaway. But in stepping back and reviewing the last 20 months of Trump II legal battles, yesterday’s developments are datapoints in favor of a tentative working theory that appeals courts are slowly coming around to the urgency of the current moment.

In the first six months of Trump II, district judges were on their heels, caught off guard by the ferocity of the rampage against the rule of law and still tethered to old norms and expectations for the Justice Department that no longer held true. It was a brutal stretch of watching the Trump administration seize some key early wins and capture important legal ground.

After being collectively kicked in the teeth, district judges pretty quickly adjusted to the new reality — but appeals courts failed to back district judges in key respects, missed the urgency of the moment, and surrendered more ground to the lawlessness.

More recently, appellate judges have begun to turn, too. Two glimmers of hope yesterday came at the appeals court level, with the en banc D.C. Circuit looking poised to allow U.S. District Judge James Boasberg to resume his contempt of court inquiry in the original Alien Enemies Act case and the 11th Circuit handing Trump a loss in his bogus settlement with the IRS.

That still leaves the Supreme Court, which — with a few notable exceptions — has been Trump’s greatest enabler. It played true to form yesterday with an emergency intervention that will allow the administration’s brutal third-country removals policy to continue past the election and until it rules after oral arguments in December.

Unlike the lower courts, the Supreme Court will not eventually come around. While we’ve already seen examples — most prominently on tariffs, birthright citizenship, and the USPS mail-in ballots rule — of the Roberts Court refusing to endorse some of Trump’s worst excesses, the high court is too deeply compromised and its six-justice right-wing majority too invested in the GOP’s partisan fate to emerge as a reliable bulwark.

But the appeals courts may buy us some additional time by slowing the speed of the descent.

A quick rundown on yesterday’s developments, in turn:

AEA Contempt Inquiry Likely to Resume

The 7-4 Democratic-Republican split on the en banc D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals already boded well for the prospect of Judge Boasberg being able to resume his inquiry into whether Trump administration officials, including DOJ lawyers, should be held in contempt of court for violating his orders to stop and turn around deportation flights under the Alien Enemies Act.

Oral arguments left the strong impression that a majority of the full court will greenlight Boasberg’s inquiry. I’d pay particular attention to Judge Karen Henderson, a Bush I appointee who authored an important ruling on the substance of the Alien Enemies Act last year in the same case.

For more, I wrote at some length about yesterday’s oral arguments here.

Trump Takes a Loss in IRS Case

A unanimous three-judge panel of the 11th Circuit declined to put on hold the sanctions order by U.S. District Judge Kathleen M. Williams in Trump’s collusive lawsuit against the IRS.

The ruling was made on procedural grounds, including that the appeal was premature given Williams hadn’t yet decided on the amount of attorney fees award in the case. But while the appeals court panel — two Obama appointees and one Trump appointee — didn’t reach the merits of Williams’ ruling it did conclude: “Given the record before us, the appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court committed clear error in its collusion and bad faith findings.”

Roberts Courts Does It Again

The Supreme Court intervened on an emergency basis to block lower court orders that had effectively frozen the Trump administration policy of deporting people without notice or hearing to countries they are not from and to which they have no connection.

The three Democratic appointees opposed granting the stay.

The decision by a federal court in Boston, and upheld by the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals, had required giving detainees a chance to voice fear of torture or persecution before being deported to third countries. Now the third-country deportations can resume with abandon.

In what legal experts called an unusual twist, the Supreme Court identified three questions it wants briefed in the case, then gave the Trump administration the chance to identify any other issues it wants addressed: “Such other questions that the Government determines are appropriate for the proper disposition of the case.”

The court fast-tracked oral arguments for December.

Victim of ICE Shooting Charged in Texas

Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, the Venezuelan national shot by an ICE agent in Austin, Texas 10 days ago, has been charged with assaulting a federal officer during their initial encounter.

Garcés Perez, who was shot in the shoulder and still has a bullet in his back, allegedly hit the ICE agent with his vehicle’s side mirror as he fled the initial traffic stop. That portion of the incident is caught on the body cam of one of the officers, according to a court filing.

Two observations about the filings:

  • The shooting came a few moments later, after an alleged high-speed chase, when only one officer — without a body cam running — was present.

  • In the court filing, a Homeland Security Investigations agent said he interviewed Garces Perez and the non-shooting agent after the incident, but gave no indication that he had interviewed the agent who fired his gun.

Swimming in Schadenfreude

The only proper way to cover the trio of Jack Smith hearings before Congress over the past year is as perjury trap under a veneer of disinformation — which is what made Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO) getting snared in his own perjury trap such a feast of mockery and memes.

If you still haven’t gotten enough:

  • TPM’s Hunter Walker: New Evidence Shows Just How Badly One Republican Senator Beclowned Himself in the Jack Smith Hearing

  • TPM’s John Light: 5 Points About a Senator’s Disastrous But Hilarious Attempt to Accuse Jack Smith of Perjury

CBP Funds Used for Pro-Trump TV Ads

The federal funds used to pay for pro-Trump TV ads airing in the stretch run of the midterm elections came from Customs and Border Protection, the WSJ reports. Outside monitors estimate some $1.4 million has been spent on the ads that have aired so far, but Democratic lawmakers claim allege that $20 million of CBP money has been shifted to the ad campaign.

Two important and deeply corrosive moves by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to politicize the military and erode its professionalism:

  • Hegseth is expected to announce today that he is cutting the number of flag officers by at least 20%. As with other Trump administration purges, the initial purge is usually only half of the equation. It’s who ultimately gets elevated in their place that cements the role of loyalists, hacks, and charlatans.

23 Years Later, The U.S. Leaves Iraq

After more than two decades of unimaginable human carnage and sunk costs in toil and treasure, the last remaining U.S. forces in Iraq are departing the country today.
